reference.source: Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: A genetically heterogeneous group of mostly autosomal recessive dystrophies presenting at birth or in early infancy with hypotonia, weakness, and often early contractures
Major subtypes include merosin (laminin alpha-2)-deficient CMD from LAMA2 variants, collagen VI-related forms (Ullrich CMD and Bethlem myopathy), and the dystroglycanopathies

The dystroglycanopathies (for example those affecting fukutin-related and related glycosylation genes) can involve the brain and eyes, as in Walker-Warburg syndrome, muscle-eye-brain disease, and Fukuyama CMD
White-matter changes on brain MRI are characteristic of merosin-deficient CMD, even when cognition is preserved
Collagen VI-related disease combines proximal weakness and joint contractures with striking distal joint hyperlaxity
Respiratory insufficiency, including nocturnal hypoventilation, is a major complication and can occur even when ambulation is retained
Diagnosis integrates the clinical and MRI findings, serum creatine kinase, muscle biopsy with immunostaining, and molecular genetic testing
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, with respiratory surveillance and support, physiotherapy, orthopaedic care for contractures and scoliosis, and feeding support
reference.pathophysiology: The congenital muscular dystrophies result from variants in genes encoding proteins of the muscle-fibre basement membrane, extracellular matrix, or the glycosylation machinery that modifies alpha-dystroglycan. Loss of laminin alpha-2 (merosin) or collagen VI weakens the link between the muscle fibre and its surrounding matrix, while defective glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan impairs its binding to matrix ligands and, in the brain, disrupts neuronal migration. These defects cause early muscle-fibre injury and dystrophic change and, in the dystroglycanopathies, associated structural brain and eye malformations. The particular protein affected determines whether disease is confined to muscle or extends to the central nervous system.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital myopathies (for example nemaline and central core myopathy)
Spinal muscular atrophy presenting in infancy
Metabolic and mitochondrial myopathies of infancy
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to detect white-matter change or structural malformation
Muscle biopsy with immunostaining for merosin, collagen VI, and glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan
Next-generation sequencing gene panel for congenital muscular dystrophy
Respiratory function and sleep studies for hypoventilation
Ophthalmological assessment where a dystroglycanopathy is suspected
redFlags: Respiratory failure or nocturnal hypoventilation, which may be disproportionate to limb weakness
Feeding difficulty with aspiration risk and failure to thrive
Seizures or signs of significant brain involvement in dystroglycanopathies
Ophthalmic complications such as severe structural eye malformation
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies enormously by subtype, from severe neonatal forms such as Walker-Warburg syndrome with early mortality to milder collagen VI-related disease compatible with prolonged survival. Respiratory involvement is often the principal determinant of outcome, so early respiratory surveillance and support are critical.
pitfalls: Assuming preserved cognition excludes brain involvement, since merosin-deficient CMD shows white-matter change without intellectual disability
Overlooking respiratory failure because a child remains ambulant
Not distinguishing subtypes, which is essential for prognosis, counselling, and surveillance
Missing the associated eye and brain anomalies of the dystroglycanopathies
Attributing neonatal hypotonia to a central cause without considering a muscle disorder
management: No cure exists; care is supportive and subtype-directed, coordinated by a specialist neuromuscular team
Proactive respiratory surveillance with sleep studies and non-invasive ventilation for nocturnal hypoventilation
Physiotherapy, stretching, orthoses and serial casting or surgery to prevent and manage contractures
Monitoring and management of scoliosis, including spinal bracing or corrective surgery
Nutritional and safe-swallowing support, with gastrostomy feeding where bulbar involvement threatens intake
Cardiac surveillance in subtypes carrying cardiomyopathy risk
Ophthalmology and developmental input where a dystroglycanopathy involves the brain and eyes
Genetic counselling and family testing given the predominantly autosomal recessive inheritance
